qs.q: Which piece of evidence is a shape clue?
o: The coastlines of South America and Africa fit like puzzle pieces
The Appalachians match mountains in Scotland
qs.why: The fit of the coastlines is the shape clue.
f: Fossils are the second clue. The shape clue is about how the outlines of the continents match.
Rocks and mountains are the third clue (Formations). The shape clue is about the coastlines.
Fossils are the second clue. The shape clue is about the coastlines.
qs.tip: Fit, Fossils, Formations (rocks).

qs.q: Mesosaurus was a freshwater reptile. Its fossils are found only in South America and Africa. What does that suggest?
o: It swam across the Atlantic Ocean
It was carried across by ships
The fossils formed in two different oceans
qs.why: It could not cross a salty ocean, so the land must have been connected.
f: Mesosaurus lived in fresh water. It could not swim across a salty ocean.
The fossils are about 280 million years old, long before ships.
It lived in fresh water, not in an ocean. The simplest explanation is that the land was joined.
qs.tip: Land animals and fresh-water animals cannot cross a wide ocean.

qs.q: The Appalachian Mountains match mountains in Scotland and Scandinavia in age and rock type. If you fit the continents together, you would see…
o: One long mountain chain that was later split apart
qs.why: The ranges line up into one long chain.
f: If they match in age and rock type, they are not unrelated. They formed together.
A trench forms when an ocean plate sinks. These are matching mountains.
The clue is matching rock type and age, which points to one chain.
qs.tip: Formations: matching rocks and mountains across the Atlantic.

qs.q: Glossopteris seeds were too heavy to blow across an ocean, yet its fossils are on five continents. What is the best explanation?
o: Those continents were joined when the plant lived
Wind blew the seeds across the ocean
qs.why: Joined continents let the plant spread over land.
f: The seeds were too heavy to blow across an ocean.
Plants cannot swim across an ocean.
These are fossils that formed long before people. The simplest explanation is joined land.
qs.tip: Fossils: the same land fossils on continents far apart.

qs.q: Using the table (500 km = 20 million years, 1,000 km = 40 million years), how old is rock 500 km from the ridge?
qs.why: 500 km out, the rock is about 20 million years old.
f: 0 million years is right at the ridge, at 0 km.
40 million years is the rock at 1,000 km.
60 million years is the rock at 1,500 km.
qs.tip: Youngest at the ridge, older with distance on both sides.

qs.q: Where is the youngest rock on the seafloor?
o: At the edge of a continent
qs.why: Youngest at the ridge, where new crust forms.
f: Rock gets older as you move away from the ridge, so the far rock is the oldest.
The ridge is where new crust forms, not the continent edge.
Age increases steadily with distance from the ridge, so halfway is middle-aged.
qs.tip: Youngest at the ridge, oldest farthest from it.

qs.q: How do the magnetic stripes on one side of a ridge compare to the other side?
o: They match like a mirror image
They only appear on one side
They get older toward the ridge
qs.why: The stripes mirror each other across the ridge.
f: The stripes follow a clear pattern that matches on both sides.
Both sides have stripes, matching each other.
Rock gets older away from the ridge, not toward it.
qs.tip: Stripes on one side match the other like a mirror image.

qs.q: Why are the stripes a mirror image?
o: New crust forms in the middle and moves away equally in both directions
Earth's field flips only on one side of the ridge
Waves wash the stripes into place
Two ridges formed side by side
qs.why: New crust forms at the center and spreads equally both ways.
f: The field flips everywhere at once. The crust that locked it in moves both ways.
Waves do not change magnetic direction locked in rock.
There is one ridge. Crust forms at it and moves outward on both sides.
qs.tip: Magnetic grains lock in Earth's field as the lava cools.

qs.q: Which order shows how seafloor spreading makes new crust?
qs.why: Magma rises, cools into crust, pushes older crust aside, and that older crust ends up farther away.
f: Magma has to rise first, then it can cool.
Crust cannot push anything until the magma has risen and cooled.
The older crust is the result at the end, not the start.
qs.tip: Rise, Cool, Push, Older.

qs.q: A rock 1,000 km from the ridge is 40 million years old. What is the spreading rate? (rate = distance ÷ age)
qs.why: 1,000 ÷ 40 = 25 km per million years (2.5 cm per year).
f: 40 is the age. You still need to divide the distance by the age.
Check the division: 1,000 ÷ 40 is 25, not 4.
Don't add. Divide the distance by the age.
qs.tip: Spreading rate = distance ÷ age.

qs.q: A spreading rate of 2.5 cm per year means the Atlantic Ocean is…
qs.why: New crust keeps forming, so the ocean widens slowly.
f: Narrower would mean plates coming together. At a ridge they move apart.
Plates are moving apart by about 2.5 cm each year, so the width changes.
The plates are moving apart, so the ocean gets wider.
qs.tip: New crust pushes older crust away on both sides.

qs.q: Each stripe in the seafloor shows…
o: When that crust formed, locking in Earth's magnetic direction
qs.why: Each stripe is a time stamp of when the crust formed.
f: Storms do not change magnetic direction in rock.
Continents colliding makes mountains, not stripes.
A fault is a crack. Stripes are bands of magnetic direction locked in as crust cooled.
qs.tip: The field flips, crust keeps forming, so each flip adds a stripe.

qs.q: Plates are moving toward each other. What type of boundary is it?
qs.why: Convergent means plates come together.
f: Divergent = Divide. Plates move apart.
Transform plates slide past each other.
A ridge is a landform at a divergent boundary, not a boundary type.
qs.tip: Divergent = Divide. Convergent = Come together. Transform = slide.

qs.q: The San Andreas Fault is an example of which boundary?
qs.why: The plates slide past each other, which is a transform boundary.
f: At divergent boundaries the plates move apart, like the Mid-Atlantic Ridge.
At convergent boundaries the plates push together, like the Himalayas.
It is a boundary. Plates slide past each other here.
qs.tip: Transform = slide. Example: San Andreas Fault.

qs.q: Where would you find a mid-ocean ridge?
qs.why: Ridges form where plates move apart and magma fills the gap.
f: Convergent boundaries make trenches, volcanoes and mountains.
Transform boundaries make faults and offset streams.
Each boundary type has its own landforms. A ridge is where plates pull apart.
qs.tip: Divergent: plates move apart. Landforms: mid-ocean ridge, rift valley.

qs.q: When two continents collide, what forms?
o: Tall mountain ranges like the Himalayas
qs.why: Neither continent sinks, so the crust crumples upward into mountains.
f: A trench forms when an ocean plate sinks. Continents do not sink.
A rift valley forms where plates pull apart.
A ridge forms where plates pull apart. This is a collision.
qs.tip: Two continents collide, neither sinks, so the crust crumples.

qs.q: Why do earthquakes and volcanoes line up around the Pacific Ocean?
qs.why: Most earthquakes and volcanoes happen along plate boundaries, like the Ring of Fire.
f: Thickness is not the cause. The location is the edge of plates.
Heat from water isn't the cause. The plate edges are where plates interact.
They do line up. It is called the Ring of Fire.
qs.tip: Look along the edges of plates.

qs.q: Which crust is more dense?
qs.why: Oceanic basalt is denser than continental granite.
f: Continental crust is the lighter one, about 2.7 g/cm³.
Oceanic crust is 3.0 and continental is 2.7. They are different.
Density is a property of the rock. It does not change.
qs.tip: Oceanic: dark basalt, dense. Continental: lighter, like granite.

qs.q: At a convergent boundary, an ocean plate meets a continental plate. Which one sinks?
qs.why: The denser oceanic crust sinks beneath the lighter continental crust.
f: Continental crust is too buoyant to be pulled down.
The denser one sinks, not both.
Plates keep moving. The denser plate goes under.
qs.tip: Dense ocean crust sinks. Light continental crust stays up.

qs.q: What is it called when one plate sinks beneath another?
qs.why: Subduction is one plate sinking beneath another. A trench forms where it bends down.
f: Spreading is plates moving apart at a ridge.
Transform means sliding sideways.
Erosion is wearing away of surface rock, not plates moving.
qs.tip: A trench forms where the plate bends down.

qs.q: Some continental rocks are nearly 4 billion years old, but no seafloor is older than about 200 million years. Why?
o: Continental crust is not recycled; ocean crust is subducted and destroyed
Continental rock is made of harder minerals
qs.why: Ocean crust is recycled at trenches. Light continental crust is not.
f: It is about density, not hardness. Light crust stays at the surface.
Seafloor forms at ridges all the time. The old parts sink at trenches.
Water does not melt the crust. Subduction destroys the old ocean crust.
qs.tip: Ocean crust gets recycled at trenches. Continental crust does not.

qs.q: Which part of an argument uses numbers or data?
qs.why: Evidence is the data or observations.
f: The claim answers the question. The data supports it.
Reasoning explains why the evidence supports the claim. The numbers themselves are the evidence.
A question starts the argument, but the data is the evidence.
qs.tip: Claim answers. Evidence is data. Reasoning explains why.

qs.q: Which is strong evidence that the seafloor is young?
o: I think the ocean looks young
Seafloor ages increase with distance from the ridge
qs.why: Measured ages are data. That makes strong evidence.
f: That's an opinion. Strong evidence uses data and measurements.
Appeals to what "everyone knows" aren't data.
How something feels isn't evidence.
qs.tip: Strong: data and observations. Weak: opinions or guesses.

qs.q: Fill in: New crust forms at ______ and old crust sinks at ______.
qs.why: New crust forms at ridges. Old crust sinks at trenches.
f: That's reversed. Ridges make new crust.
Ridges make new crust. Continents are not where it forms.
Ridges make new crust. Old ocean crust sinks at trenches, not at continents.
qs.tip: Ridges make crust. Trenches destroy it.

qs.q: Which reasoning best connects the evidence to the claim "the seafloor is younger than the continents"?
o: Dense ocean crust sinks at trenches, but light continental crust is too buoyant to sink
The ocean is bigger than the land
qs.why: Reasoning explains why: ocean crust is destroyed, continental crust survives.
f: Size doesn't explain why one is younger.
Agreement isn't reasoning. Reasoning explains why the evidence supports the claim.
Rock color doesn't explain age. Reasoning links evidence to the claim.
qs.tip: Reasoning explains why the evidence supports the claim.
